title: ABSTRACT
summary: A declassified FTD report (CR-20-13-69 INT, Vol I) on tactical evaluation of a Soviet MiG-21F-13 (FISHBED E) against USN and USAF fighters, covering performance, flight tests, systems, design features, and exploitation results. It confirms published estimates and validates current tactics. Contents list: summary, supplements, Annexes A-D (tactical mission, maintenance, cockpit, weapon effects), Attachments 1-5 (test aircraft, F-4D, F-105D, F-105F), references, acronyms, and illustrations of cockpit, ejection, and radar/compressor behavior.

nodes.summary: Comparative tactical analysis of the F-4 and MIG-21 (FISHBED). The F-4 can defeat the MIG-21 below 15,000 feet by exploiting its airspeed limit and bleed-off at high G, attacking its blind cone, and fighting in the vertical. nodes.summary: Guidance for air-combat engagements against the MiG-21: establish maximum angle-off and high total closure angle (TCA) at initial sighting and maintain it using minimum G to avoid airspeed bleed-off; maneuver in a vertical plane below 15,000 feet, avoid slow-speed reversals and prolonged close-in turning fights, and disengage if needed to keep energy for reattack; exploit the MiG-21's 50-degree rear-hemisphere blind cone using lag pursuit or rolling maneuvers; the MiG-21 is hard to see, so visual scanning must be emphasized in high-threat areas, with #2 and #4 wingmen focusing primarily on scanning during engagements.

F-4 vs MIG-21: high-speed disengagement, accelerate, increase separation, and set up head-on attacks when conditions allow, otherwise fully disengage. F-105: maintain max airspeed above 450 KIAS in high-threat areas, avoid prolonged maneuvering, don't let airspeed bleed below 450 KCAS, and rely on warnings since APR-25 gear may not warn of MIG-21 missiles; MIG-21 is hard to see visually. With a 50-knot closure rate, press the attack; otherwise separate via descending acceleration. Exploit the MIG-21's 50-degree rear blind cone with lag pursuit or rolling maneuvers. F-111: avoid maneuvering fights, accelerate and separate at first sign of attack, and use hit-and-run only when a favorable offensive position exists.

nodes.summary: Describes MIG-21 flight test mission rules: a chase aircraft pilot familiar with aircraft and emergency procedures was required on every mission; a mobile control officer familiar with MIG-21 operation was on duty for all flights; tests were day VFR only; drag chutes were used on landings; ground taxiing was minimized by towing the aircraft to the runway and to the hangar after shutdown. Mission priorities were set: low/medium altitude ACM and comparative performance against F-4D/E and F-105D/F, then quantitative performance, stability and control, and energy maneuverability testing, then continued ACM against selected tactical aircraft. nodes.summary: Describes MIG-21 vs F-4 comparisons: MIG-21 suffers severe airframe buffet at .92-.98 IMN below 15,000 ft, making it unusable as a weapon until speed is reduced. Zoom tests show F-4 superior to MIG-21 in most configurations, especially subsonic, despite data suggesting MIG-21 superiority above 20,000 ft. Turn tests show MIG-21 generates more G at a given speed but loses airspeed faster; F-4 wins 180-degree turns by about 20 KIAS. ACM tactics: F-4 should keep high airspeed, play the vertical, and force fights below 15,000 ft; in four spiral tests F-4 denied MIG-21 kills.

(e) Radar Signature:
nodes.summary: Describes MiG-21 radar signature tests with F-4 aircraft (24 intercept sorties): smallest cross section head-on; detection/lock ranges rise from head-on (20/15 NM) to tail-on (25/17 NM) to beam (35/28 NM). APQ-109 (F-4D) detected 5-10% farther than APQ-120 (F-4E), due to wider beam from redesigned reflector. Neither F-4 variant has low-altitude/look-down capability, so both are vulnerable to low front-quarter and head-on attacks; visual lookout remains the primary threat sensor. APQ-120 automatic acquisition range gate maxes at 12,500 ft, making it of limited use in practice and increasing need for crew coordination. Recommends extending it to 30,000 ft. Also covers unloaded acceleration above 0.96 Mach below 15,000 ft for disengagement and reversing after 2-3 NM with all-aspect missiles if re-engagement is desired.

nodes.title: (f) Radar Technique and Discussion.
nodes.summary: Compares radar search modes of the F-4D's APQ-120 and APQ-109. MAP B mode gives slightly longer detection range than RDR 1 Bar but a slightly lower detection probability due to its tight beam. RDR 3 Bar is likely ineffective because targets are illuminated infrequently. The APQ-120 RDR mode has a 6.7 degree beam versus 4.7 degrees for the APQ-109, so long-range targets fill little of the beam and sweep. Targets are distorted in the B sweep until strong signal returns, so they are easily mistaken for receiver noise. Best results come from the APQ-120 MAP mode.

nodes.title: (2) F-105
nodes.summary: Compares F-105 and MiG-21 in a flight evaluation. Acceleration is roughly equal under stated conditions, with the MiG-21 slightly ahead. The MiG-21 has better turn performance at all airspeeds above 540 KIAS, plus superior instantaneous and sustained G capability. ACM tests advise the F-105 not to pursue a maneuvering fight, and to separate by accelerating past 595 KCAS below 15,000 ft. The APR-25 RHAW detected MiG-21 radar lock-ons only within about 3.5 km and missed some passes, so visual lookout remains the primary detection method.

nodes.title: (3) F121
nodes.summary: F-111 Mission 27 found that an immediate turn at maximum MiG detection range, followed by low-magnitude jinking acceleration to minimum altitude and maximum Mach, was the only effective defensive maneuver. APS-109 was evaluated on Mission 99 against the MiG-21 range-only radar: it gives audio and strobe indications on lock-on, with max detection 5 km and average 3.5 km (about 11,484 ft, inside ATOLL range). It aids detection but should not be the primary means; visual look-around and scan remain best.

nodes.title: (4) F100
nodes.summary: Evaluation of the F-100 versus MIG-21 in mission 25. The F-100 can escape close-in gun attacks with high-G reversals, but this is a last-ditch tactic and a follow-up MIG-21 attack would succeed. The MIG-21 limits F-100 separation to 595 KIAS below 15,000 ft. Flight integrity, teamwork, and lookout are key; F-100 should avoid engagements when conditions are not optimal. The MIG-21 has a slight turn advantage at all tested speeds and altitudes, and far better sustained G.

nodes.title: (5) F65N.
nodes.summary: Comparative flight evaluation of US aircraft against the MIG-21. F-5N: acceleration superior at low altitude up to MIG-21 Q limit, MIG-21 better unloaded acceleration to 1.2 Mach; zoom slightly favors F-5N at 0.9 Mach; turn capability comparable (MIG-21 more instantaneous G, F-5N better sustained G); in ACM, visual acquisition difficult and outcomes driven by pilot proficiency; F-5N useful as MIG-21 training surrogate. RF-101: acceleration equal subsonic, MIG-21 faster in afterburner acceleration; RF-101 should accelerate and dive to separate from attacker. B-66: MIG-21 far superior in acceleration; high-G descending spiral fails to defeat attack, escort recommended. RF-4C: QRC-353A effective in denying radar range information to MIG-21.

nodes.title: F-5 vs MIG-21 and RF-101, B-66 Combat Performance Comparison
nodes.summary: Compares F-5 and MIG-21 performance: closely matched acceleration, zoom, and turn capability, with pilot proficiency decisive; F-5 exceeds MIG-21 low-altitude Q limit, has better cockpit visibility, and is a good training stand-in for MIG-21 combat. RF-101 vs MIG-21 (mission 68): equal subsonic acceleration, MIG-21 faster in afterburner; RF-101 can exceed MIG-21 Q limit below 15,000 ft; MIG-21 turns superior; RF-101 under attack should accelerate, dive, and separate. B-66 (mission 78): MIG-21 far superior in acceleration; high-G spiral failed to escape attack, so fighter escort is recommended.

nodes.title: (8) RF-4C.
nodes.summary: The QRC-353A chaff dispenser was evaluated on mission 98 during a limited test against a MiG-21 attacking an RF-4C. When the MiG-21 Range-Only Radar locked on and the chaff was activated, radar lock transferred to the chaff, denying the MiG-21 range information. The pilot could still make an effective ATOLL missile and follow-up gun attack using visual range estimation or manual sight ranging.

nodes.title: B, MIG-21 Cockpit Evaluation
nodes.summary: Evaluation of the MIG-21F-13 cockpit: Soviet engineering simplicity, poor switch and instrument grouping, cluttered layout, and minimal ground support (over-wing refueling, battery starts). Covers the entry ladder, seat and parachute harness, marginal seat comfort, poor taxi visibility, and head clearance. Also covers the pneumatic canopy (no unlocked warning, a forceful-opening incident), inconsistent switch placards, scattered armament controls, poorly grouped and dim warning lights, console and pedestal ratings, emergency controls, stick grip buttons, and throttle quadrant ratings.

nodes.title: C, FISHBED E Armament and Fire Control. Systems
nodes.summary: Evaluation of the FISHBED E (MiG-21) armament and fire control: poor forward visibility hampers target acquisition; switchology is adequate for air-to-ground but excessive for air-to-air, though a missile-to-gun switch takes one movement. The NR-30 30mm cannon holds 60 rounds, fires about 4.2 seconds, with pipper jitter near 20 mils and muzzle flash visible at 3 miles; a bulldozer test showed 2 hits rendered it irreparable, with no malfunctions. Gunsight issues include hard manual ranging, gyro drift above 2.5 G, sluggish electrical caging, and a 94-mil depression limit. Desirable MiG-21F-13 features are also covered: maintenance simplicity, pilot workload reduction, small frontal size, and light weight.

nodes.summary: Covers the MIG-21 FISHBED E evaluation: a simple, reliable Mach 2 jet with no major maintenance issues over 102 flights (minor EGT problems, a small hydraulic leak, landing gear and canopy concerns). Servicing was minimal, with six men needing about 30 minutes between flights and self-contained electrical start. Systems were unsophisticated but reliable, corrosion-free, and quiet in the cockpit. Pilot seating may add about 1g of g tolerance. Cockpit visibility was poor, with a 50-degree rear blind cone. Cockpit layout, parachute harness, and switch placement were rated poor. Instrument grouping was poor, though engine instruments were good.

nodes.summary: Tactical guidance for fighting a MiG-21 with F-4/F-8 aircraft: fly combat spread and engage as a section, since the MiG-21 is small and hard to see and is usually under GCI control. Keep 450+ KIAS while patrolling and maintain high energy in the fight, trading airspeed for altitude rather than slow scissors. Force the fight below 16,000 ft to exploit the MiG-21's speed and stick-force limits. Use lag pursuit at 3,000-5,000 ft astern, outside its turn radius, to stay in its blind cone. Avoid overshoots with hit-and-run attacks and high yo-yos, and use high-g roll-away if an overshoot looms. Use oblique loops for reciprocal turns below 16,000 ft.

nodes.summary: Conclusions on MIG-21 versus F-4/F-8 in air combat maneuvering (ACM): the MIG-21 is hard to visually track, has a tactical edge from small size, high maneuverability at high g and low speed, Mach 2 capability at altitude, and buffet above 16,000 ft. Its turn performance is impressive due to low thrust-to-weight, but it suffers high stick forces and airspeed bleed-off below 400 KIAS. Zoom performance is inferior to the F-4 below 25,000 ft, with center-line tank configuration comparable. Gunsight has limitations, total performance degrades with Sidewinder missiles, engine acceleration is slow, and it leaves little smoke. Cockpit visibility is seriously degraded aft. The 30 mm cannon is effective; the aircraft is vulnerable, easy to maintain, with high sortie rate and 30-minute recycle. F-4/F-8 have a tactical disadvantage due to size and smoke, and better acceleration at low and medium altitudes.

summary: Foreign Technology Division (AFSC, Wright-Patterson AFB) report CR-35-13-59 on a tactical exploitation of a Soviet FISHBED B (MIG-21F-13) flown 23 Jan-8 Apr 1968.
